summary.title: Clean Architecture
summary.one_liner: Robert C. Martin's book on applying SOLID principles and component-level design to structure software so that business logic stays independent of frameworks, databases and UI.
keywords: how to structure a software application
takeaways: Software architecture is built on design principles such as SOLID, applied at the component and system level.
The book presents Martin's Clean Architecture pattern, which compares to Cockburn's Hexagonal Architecture, and keeps business logic independent of frameworks and infrastructure.
Architecture questions covered include high-level structures for web, database, thick-client, console and embedded apps.
Reviewers note the book mixes general SOLID principles with one specific proposed pattern, and that the first half is largely familiar from earlier Martin books.
Reviews are mixed: many find it useful for experienced developers and architects, while others find it repetitive, anecdotal or light on practical code examples.
summary.summary: This 432-page book by Robert C. Martin ("Uncle Bob") follows Clean Code and The Clean Coder and aims to bring discipline to application architecture and design. The publisher blurb lists the questions it addresses, including the best high-level structures for different application types, the core principles of architecture and design, the role of the architect, and how designs go wrong. The Goodreads page itself contains mostly reader reviews, which describe the book as a mix of SOLID-based architecture principles and a deep dive into Martin's own Clean Architecture pattern, with a personal appendix and few practical code samples. Reviewers disagree on its value, with several finding it repetitive or anecdotal and others finding it a useful refresher for architects.
